---
title: "Quiz: diffusion priors for inverse problems"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** With a Gaussian prior, MAP, posterior mean and Tikhonov coincide. Why do they separate with a learned prior of cell images?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the posterior of a Gaussian look like, and that of a mixture?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A Gaussian posterior has one peak, at its mean. A realistic prior gives a posterior with several separate possibilities (one nucleolus or two, one spot or two): the mean averages them (blurry), the most probable image picks one, and samples pick each with its probability.
:::

---

**Q2.** What is the null space of a microscope, in one sentence, and who fills it in a diffusion-based restoration?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Invisible objects; the cut-off.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Everything the measurement cannot see, e.g. structure finer than the cut-off; in the restoration it comes entirely from the prior.
:::

---

**Q3.** A restored image has a residual that looks like noise of exactly the right size. Is the restoration correct?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the residual see?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily: consistency is necessary but not sufficient. Any change in the null space leaves the residual unchanged, so a hallucinated detail below the resolution passes the check.
:::

---

**Q4.** Several posterior samples of a restoration disagree strongly in one region. What does that tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Who decides there?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The data do not decide that region; the prior does. Do not measure details there. (Agreement is no guarantee either: all samples can agree on a wrong answer when the prior is wrong.)
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is the usual "clean-estimate" posterior sampler over-confident, especially at the start of sampling?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How certain is the clean estimate at high noise?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It checks the measurement against the current clean estimate as if it were certain, ignoring how uncertain that estimate is. At high noise it is very uncertain, so the push towards the data is far too strong; samples fit the data (and its noise) too well and are too similar.
:::

---

**Q6.** A virtual-staining model was trained on untreated cells. You apply it to treated cells whose marker doubled in intensity, with no visible change in transmitted light. What will the prediction show?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What can the model know?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Untreated intensity: the input does not show the change, and the training data never had it. The treatment effect vanishes, and the samples agree, so nothing warns you.
:::

---

**Q7.** A method's 90 % bands contain the truth 75 % of the time on test images. What does that mean?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Coverage.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The bands are too narrow (over-confident): the prior does not match these images, or the sampler is approximate. Its uncertainty statements cannot be taken at face value.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Scalar prior $\mathcal N(0, 4)$, noise variance 1. Which λ makes Tikhonov $\arg\min (y - x)^2 + \lambda x^2$ equal to the posterior mean, and what is the estimate for $y = 1$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\lambda = \sigma_n^2/s^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\lambda = 1/4$; estimate $y/(1 + \lambda) = 0.8$, the Wiener gain $4/5$.
:::
